ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Cerebral blood flow (CBF) is the amount of blood reaching brain tissue each minute. Autoregulation keeps CBF stable despite blood pressure changes, but failure leads to ischemia or edema.

b: Autoregulation maintains flow between MAP 50‑150 mmHg

t.b: Does the patient have reduced flow velocity? Low velocity suggests hypoperfusion; high velocity may indicate vasospasm.
Is there a region of low cerebral blood volume? Low CBV indicates ischemic core; preserved CBV with delayed Tmax suggests penumbra.
Is cortical oxygenation low? Low rSO₂ supports global hypoperfusion; normal values may mask deep brain ischemia.

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical impact and imaging: mild (symptomatic but reversible), moderate (persistent deficits), severe (coma or infarction).
b: Mild: transient syncope, dizziness
Moderate: focal neurological deficit, altered consciousness >1 h
Severe: coma, irreversible infarction on imaging

sections.p: Reduced CBF can be arterial, venous, or systemic. In low‑resource settings, infectious and hematologic disorders are common contributors.
b: Cardiac output failure (e.g., severe heart block, Stokes‑Adams attacks)
Severe hypotension (septic shock, hemorrhage)
Hypercapnia or hypocapnia‑induced vasoconstriction
Infectious vasculitis (TB meningitis, neurosyphilis)
Sickle cell vaso‑occlusion
Severe anemia or polycythemia
Intracranial hypertension (malaria cerebral edema, TB meningitis)
Herbal toxins causing vasospasm

sections.p: Patients may present with sudden loss of consciousness, focal weakness, headache, or seizures, depending on the speed and region of flow loss.
b: Syncope with rapid recovery (hypotension, arrhythmia)
Gradual confusion, headache (global hypoperfusion)
Focal motor deficit (territorial ischemia)
Seizures (cortical irritation from edema)

sections.p: Choose tests that answer the physiologic question: is flow reduced, why, and where?

t.b: Is systemic pressure adequate for autoregulation? MAP <50 mmHg suggests risk of CBF failure.
Is PaCO₂ low (hypocapnia) causing vasoconstriction? PaCO₂ <35 mmHg → reduced CBF.
Is there arrhythmia causing intermittent cerebral perfusion? Complete heart block → Stokes‑Adams attacks.
Is there infarction, edema, or mass effect compromising flow? Diffusion restriction = ischemic core.
Is CSF showing TB or bacterial meningitis that can cause vasculitis? Elevated protein, low glucose support diagnosis.

sections.p: Unchecked CBF loss quickly leads to irreversible brain injury.
b: Persistent coma >6 h
New focal deficit with worsening imaging
Seizure refractory to treatment
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, Cushing triad)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then support perfusion and prevent secondary injury.
b: Restore MAP 70‑90 mmHg (fluids, vasopressors) to stay within autoregulatory range
Correct hypocapnia: give controlled ventilation or CO₂ supplementation
Treat arrhythmias: temporary pacing for complete heart block
Antimicrobial therapy for TB, bacterial meningitis, or malaria
Transfusion for severe anemia or sickle cell crisis
Manage intracranial pressure: head elevation, osmotherapy, avoid hyperventilation

sections.p: Monitor neurologic status, repeat imaging, and address chronic risk factors.
b: Serial neurological exams every 4 h in acute phase
Repeat CT/MRI at 24‑48 h if deterioration
Control hypertension, treat cardiac disease, vaccinate against meningitis

sections.p: Conditions that mimic CBF reduction but have different mechanisms.
b: Syncope from neurocardiogenic reflex (normal CBF)
Seizure post‑ictal confusion (neuronal hyper‑activity, not hypoperfusion)
Migraine aura (cortical spreading depression, transient CBF change)

sections.p: Some measurements appear normal despite serious hypoperfusion.
b: Normal MAP in severe anemia: oxygen delivery still low
Normal PaCO₂ with cerebral vasospasm (e.g., after subarachnoid hemorrhage)
CT may miss early ischemia; diffusion MRI is more sensitive

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness lasting >1 min

faq.q: Why does low CO₂ reduce cerebral blood flow?
faq.a: Hypocapnia causes cerebral arteriolar smooth‑muscle constriction, lowering vessel diameter and flow.

faq.q: What is the autoregulatory range of MAP?
faq.a: Between roughly 50 and 150 mmHg; outside this range flow becomes pressure‑dependent.

faq.q: Can a normal blood pressure guarantee adequate brain perfusion?
faq.a: No; anemia, hypoxia, or vasospasm can impair delivery even with normal pressure.

exam: Explain how cerebral autoregulation protects the brain and list its limits.
A patient with complete heart block presents with fainting. Describe the pathophysiology linking the arrhythmia to cerebral blood flow loss.
Interpret a CT perfusion map showing reduced CBV but prolonged Tmax in a patient with malaria.
